extracted.intended_audience: employers, industry stakeholders, state agencies, and public commenters on OSHA's proposed heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytic methods OSHA uses in the NPRM to determine which employers, establishments, and employees are within scope of the proposed heat standard and to estimate counts of affected entities and employees by region, industry, work condition, and shift. Includes definitions of exemptions and the datasets/assumptions used to operationalize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope applicability and exclusive-workforce exemption
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed standard would apply to all employers in the identified industries unless the workforce is exclusively performing work activities that meet one or more specific exemption definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employees (and employers) are out of scope if their workforce exclusively performs any of the following: (1) work activities for which there is no reasonable expectation of exposure at or above the initial heat trigger; (2) work activities where the employee is exposed to temperatures above the initial heat trigger for fifteen minutes or less in any sixty-minute period; (3) emergency response activities of workplace emergency response teams or any emergency response activities already covered under specified OSHA standards (29 CFR 1910.120, 1910.146, 1910.156, part 1915 subpart P, 1926.65, 1926.1211); (4) work activities performed in indoor work areas or vehicles where air conditioning consistently keeps ambient temperature below 80 °F; (5) telework; and (6) sedentary work activities in indoor work areas where the work only involves some combination of sitting, occasional standing and walking for brief periods, and occasional lifting of objects weighing less than ten pounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: No reasonable expectation of exposure (method for identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA treats employees working in 'Indoors, Environmentally Controlled' settings (per O*NET) as out of scope under the 'no reasonable expectation' exemption unless they are exposed to process heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses O*NET classifications to identify these employees and, combined with other exemptions, assumes no additional adjustments are necessary for this exemption. Comments are requested if stakeholders disagree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: Short-duration exposure (definition and estimation method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Short-duration exposure is defined as being exposed to temperatures above the initial heat trigger for fifteen minutes or less in any sixty-minute period. OSHA estimates counts of such employees primarily using the ORS dataset and OEWS-derived percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For indoor settings OSHA uses OEWS percentages of employees 'not exposed' and 'seldomly exposed' to extreme heat as reflective of the short-duration exemption; for outdoor settings OSHA uses percentages of employees who do not work outdoors or seldom work outdoors. OSHA multiplies the percentage of industry employment in each SOC occupation by the summation of these exposure percentages for that occupation, aggregates to 4-digit NAICS industries, and uses 2-digit NAICS sector averages when 4-digit data are missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: Emergency response activities (scope and data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations whose primary function is firefighting, emergency response activities of workplace emergency teams, EMS, technical search and rescue, and any emergency response activities covered under specific OSHA standards are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To identify exempt career firefighters OSHA used the USFA National Fire Department Registry, treating each recorded fire department as a firm and each fire station as an establishment; employment counts are active career firefighters only (volunteer and paid-on-call excluded). OSHA requests comment on whether additional establishments/employees should be out of scope and on alternative methodologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: Sedentary indoor work (definition and estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sedentary work activities are defined consistent with ORS/occupation strength data (work where required strength is considered sedentary); employees performing only sedentary indoor work as defined are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses ORS percent-sedentary estimates by SOC, multiplies the percentage of total industry employment in an occupation by the percent sedentary in that SOC, aggregates to 4-digit NAICS, and uses sector averages for missing 4-digit data. Data coverage gaps (not all SOC codes have estimates) are noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: Telework (treatment and data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees working remotely are considered exempt from the proposed standard; hybrid employees are considered exempt during teleworking periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA applied 2022 BLS Business Response Survey (BRS) percentages of remote, on-site, and hybrid employment by sector to employment counts. OSHA assumes many teleworkers overlap with sedentary exemptions and does not always make additional separate adjustments for telework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: Indoor areas maintained below 80 °F (definition and estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work activities performed in indoor work areas or vehicles where air conditioning consistently keeps ambient temperature below 80 °F (26.7 °C) are exempt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used EIA CBECS data to estimate buildings with at least 51% cooled floorspace as qualifying establishments, assumed employees likely work in environmentally controlled floorspace regardless of percent cooled, mapped building activities to sectors, applied estimates to counts of establishments and firms, and invited comments on whether the 51% assumption is reasonable or alternatives exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption: Employees working in cooled vehicle cabs (identification and assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who work in vehicles with sufficiently cooled vehicle cabs are considered exempt from outdoor-heat exposure counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA first estimated percent of employees working in vehicles by NAICS using occupation shares (drivers). It designated a list of SOC codes as occupations primarily involving driving and multiplied industry employment percentages in those codes by the assumed percent of drivers in sufficiently cooled cabs. In absence of data OSHA assumed 34% of postal service drivers and 50% of other delivery drivers have sufficiently cooled cabs; OSHA requests better data on cooled-cab percentages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional exemption based on State Plan status
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of public entities is in-scope only if located in OSHA State Plan States; public entities in non-State Plan States (and their employees) are out of federal OSHA's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA lists the States and territories with State Plans (Alaska, Arizona, California, etc.) and uses that list to adjust counts. Stakeholders should note jurisdictional differences when estimating affected public-sector employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment methodology for overlapping exemptions and aggregation
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA accounts for overlap across exemptions (e.g., telework, sedentary, indoor environmental control) through a sequential adjustment methodology to avoid double-counting exempt employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method steps include: (1) exclude public-sector employees outside OSHA jurisdiction; (2) apply percent-sedentary to indoor, not-environmentally-controlled employees (sedentary exemption applies regardless of climate control); (3) assume most teleworkers are captured in sedentary counts and do not separately adjust for them; (4) apply ORS extreme-heat exposure percentages to indoor environmentally-controlled employees to capture process heat; (5) adjust outdoor percentages to remove short-duration exposures; (6) aggregate percentages for each 4-digit NAICS industry and use sector averages when 4-digit OEWS data are missing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating affected employees by work shift (definitions and mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA estimates employees by shift because obligations vary with heat-index triggers; it uses ATUS 2017-2018 to map work-schedule groups into three shift categories: daytime, evening, overnight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mapping: 'daytime' corresponds to ATUS regular daytime (majority of time 6 a.m.–6 p.m.) and OSHA assumes daytime employees work 8 a.m.–4 p.m.; 'evening' corresponds to majority 2 p.m.–midnight and OSHA assumes 4 p.m.–midnight; 'overnight' corresponds to majority 9 p.m.–8 a.m. and OSHA assumes midnight–8 a.m. Additional ATUS shift groups (rotating, irregular, split shift) are evenly distributed across the three categories. OSHA provides counts by region and work condition for each shift.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimating affected entities and industry profiles (NAICS breakdowns)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA produces regional and industry (4-digit NAICS) counts of affected entities, establishments, and employees across core and non-core industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables present entities/establishments/employees by core industry and region. OSHA derives these profiles using Census Bureau data, USDA, USFA, BLS datasets and documents assumptions and sources for each industry grouping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determining entity size (small and very small definitions and aggregation)
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA determines which firms/establishments are 'small' per SBA 13 CFR 121.201 and the RFA, using employment- or revenue-based thresholds by 6-digit NAICS; 'very small' is defined as firms with fewer than 20 employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because OSHA's analysis is at the 4-digit NAICS level it aggregates 6-digit SUSB counts to 4-digit. For employee-based SBA thresholds OSHA sums all economic data within employee-class sizes below the SBA cut-off; for revenue-based thresholds OSHA sums data for employee-class sizes under the largest class where average revenue per firm is under the SBA cut-off. When SUSB lacks data for a 4-digit industry OSHA uses alternative sources (Census Agriculture, QCEW) or sector averages to estimate size distributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for identifying small-government entities and fire department adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Public entities are 'small governments' if they serve populations less than 50,000; OSHA adjusts counts of small governments and fire departments accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used Census GUS local government data to determine populations served by 38,736 local governments and identified those in State Plan States and with population <50,000. For fire departments OSHA estimated median population served per fire department employee using Firehouse Magazine surveys and applied those ratios to the USFA registry to estimate which departments serve <50k and the associated employee counts; those counts were removed from affected small-government tallies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing or suppressed data and substitution rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Where 4-digit NAICS data are missing in OEWS or SUSB due to disclosure or coverage, OSHA substitutes sector (2-digit NAICS) averages or uses alternate datasets to estimate percentages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for missing OEWS occupation-exposure percentages OSHA uses 2-digit NAICS sector averages; for missing size-class data OSHA uses SUSB sector distributions or Census of Agriculture for agricultural NAICS; QCEW is used for some remaining industries. OSHA documents which alternative source was used for which industry and invites comments on better methodologies or sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: List and identification of driver SOC codes for cooled-vehicle analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA identifies specific SOC occupation codes it considers to represent occupations that involve driving vehicles exposed to outdoor heat for most work activities; these are used to estimate drivers and cooled-cab exemptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SOC codes listed include Postal Service Mail Carriers (43-5052); Agricultural Equipment Operators (45-2091); Paving/Surfacing/Tamping Equipment Operators (47-2071); Pile Driver Operators (47-2072); Operating Engineers (47-2073); Ambulance Drivers and Attendants (53-3011); Driver/Sales Workers (53-3031); Heavy Truck Drivers (53-3032); Light Truck Drivers (53-3033); School Bus Drivers (53-3051); Transit/Intercity Bus Drivers (53-3052); Shuttle Drivers and Chauffeurs (53-3053); Taxi Drivers (53-3054); Refuse and Recyclable Material Collectors (53-7081). OSHA multiplies industry employment percentage in these SOCs by assumed cooled-cab percentages (postal 34%; other delivery 50%) to estimate exempt drivers and reports in-scope driver counts by region.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data sources, documentation, and invitation for comment
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA explicitly documents the numerous data sources (e.g., BLS OEWS, ORS, ATUS, BRS; Census Bureau; EIA CBECS; USDA; USFA; Firehouse Magazine; Hooker and Baker) and assumptions used in the exposure and entity estimates, and invites public comment and alternative data/methodologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables throughout the section cite sources. OSHA repeatedly states it 'welcomes comment' on estimates, assumptions (e.g., 51% cooled floorspace threshold, cooled-cab percentages), and on whether additional establishments or employees should be considered out of scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting caveat: rounding and overlap notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tables include notes that figures may not sum exactly due to rounding and that employees may fit multiple exemption types so simple sums across exemption-type columns may overstate unique exempt employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes overlapping exemption memberships (e.g., office workers may be indoor-environmental control, sedentary, and telework) and that the total number of exempt employees is less than the simple summation across exemption types; analysts should account for overlaps when interpreting totals.
